items.prompt: Grootfontein Farm Feeds sells to farmers on 30-day credit while paying its own suppliers in cash on delivery. Explain how this arrangement could lead to a cash shortage even in months when sales are strong.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: where the business sells on credit but pays suppliers immediately, the money from each sale leaves a 30-day gap before it arrives. Mechanism: strong sales in a month mean stock must be bought and paid for at once, because suppliers are paid on delivery, while the revenue from those sales is still owed and not yet cash. Consequence for the business: outflows run weeks ahead of inflows, so the bank balance can fall towards zero - or below - even while the order book is full, which puts wage payments, supplier relationships and the survival of the business at risk.

Mechanism: award for the how - payment leaves the business immediately while the matching cash arrives 30 days later.
Consequence: award for the effect on the business - the balance falls despite strong sales - and a second consequence for the stakeholder group at risk: wages, suppliers, survival of the business.

items.prompt: Explain the features that make cash important to a business's day-to-day running.
items.canonical_answer: The features that make cash central: it is what actually settles each bill - wages, rent, supplier invoices - because a payment falls due on a date and needs money available that day; it is the most liquid resource a business holds, since stock must still be sold and debtors must still pay before they become cash; and a shortage of it shows up immediately in missed payments and lost goodwill, whatever the business earns on paper. What it includes above all is the ability to pay on time, which keeps suppliers, workers and landlords willing to keep dealing with the business.
marking_guidance: Features: award one mark for each element - cash settles dated bills, it is the most liquid resource, shortages strike immediately - and one mark for developing what the feature means for the business's daily running.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "A profitable business cannot run out of cash." Explain the error in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The error is treating profit and cash as the same measure. In fact a business earns profit when a sale is made, but the cash can arrive weeks later if the customer buys on credit, so a profitable month can end with too little cash to pay the wages - the two differ in timing. The test that separates them: ask which clock the figure is on. Profit is earned over time as value is created; cash is what can be spent today. A road-catering firm can be profitable on every contract and still miss a payroll in February, because the client pays in April.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact profit is earned at the point of sale while the cash may follow on credit, so profitable businesses can run short of cash - the timing differs.
Award the second mark for the test that separates the confused pair: which clock the figure is on.

items.prompt: Luderitz Book Corner opens June with a bank balance of N$2 000. It expects cash inflows of N$9 000 and cash outflows of N$7 500 in June. Calculate the closing balance for June.
items.canonical_answer: Formula: the closing balance is the opening balance plus net cash flow, and net cash flow is total inflows less total outflows. Substitution: 9 000 - 7 500 = N$1 500, so the net cash flow is N$1 500; then 2 000 + 1 500 = N$3 500. Units: Namibian dollars - the closing balance is N$3 500. Interpretation: the bookshop expects its cash to grow by N$1 500 over June and to finish the month with N$3 500 available, which means June is expected to be a comfortable month rather than a tight one.

Substitution: award for the working - 9 000 - 7 500 for the net cash flow, then adding the opening balance of N$2 000.
Units: the figures are Namibian dollars; the closing balance must carry the currency.
Interpretation: award for saying what N$3 500 means - the cash the business expects to hold at the end of June, N$1 500 more than it started with.

items.prompt: Explain the main parts of a simple monthly cash-flow forecast and how the parts fit together.
items.canonical_answer: The parts: an opening balance, the cash held at the start of the month; the expected cash inflows, such as cash sales and payments from debtors; the expected cash outflows, such as wages, rent and materials; the net cash flow, inflows less outflows; and the closing balance, the opening balance plus the net cash flow. What makes the parts fit together is the carry-forward: each month's closing balance becomes the next month's opening balance, so the forecast reads as one continuous position across the months rather than five separate rows.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - opening balance, inflows, outflows, net cash flow, closing balance - and one mark for what joins them: the closing balance carried forward as the next opening balance.

items.canonical_answer: The error is reading the forecast as an earnings statement. The test that separates the two: ask whether the figure came from money moving in and out, or from value earned over time. Profit is measured on sales less costs; the closing balance is measured on payments.

items.prompt: Explain the features of amending a cash-flow forecast properly.
items.canonical_answer: Done properly, an amendment has three features. It changes the underlying figure first - the new outflow or inflow in the month it lands - rather than adjusting a closing balance by hand. It recomputes the month's net cash flow from the changed inflow or outflow, so the rows stay consistent with each other. And it carries the new closing balance forward into every later month's opening balance, so what the amendment includes is the full path of the change, not just the month where it happened; a change made in one month and left there would quietly misstate every month that follows.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - change the source figure, recompute net cash flow, carry the closing balance forward - and one mark for what a proper amendment includes: the full path across later months.

items.prompt: Explain how an overdraft helps a business facing a short-term cash-flow problem.
items.canonical_answer: The benefit is speed and fit. An overdraft can be arranged before the shortage lands, and once the limit is agreed the business spends as it needs to, which means wages and supplier payments are met on time even in the trough month. Because interest runs on the amount used rather than the whole limit, the cost matches the size of the gap and stops as soon as the balance recovers, so the business borrows for weeks rather than years. That leads to the deeper benefit: the shortage passes without damage to goodwill - workers, suppliers and landlords are paid, and the business's reputation for paying its way survives a bad month.
marking_guidance: Developed benefit: award for the mechanism - spending beyond the balance up to an agreed limit - developed because interest runs on the amount used, which leads to the consequence that payments are met and goodwill survives the trough.

items.prompt: Explain one limitation of relying on an overdraft to solve a cash-flow problem.
items.canonical_answer: An overdraft is a bridge, and its limitation is that it treats the symptom rather than the cause. Because the borrowing simply covers the gap, nothing in the business's inflows or outflows has changed, so where the shortage is structural - a slide in the balances month after month - the overdraft is drawn again each month and the interest keeps building, which leads to a debt that grows while the underlying problem does not. A bank is also likely to review or recall the limit, because the bank can renegotiate the agreement, so the facility may not still be there if the slide continues - the remedy is temporary by nature, which a business with a permanent gap cannot afford to forget.
marking_guidance: Developed limitation: award for the reason - borrowing changes no flow - developed because interest builds on repeated use, which leads to the consequence that a structural shortage turns into growing debt.

items.prompt: Explain the features of the ways a business might overcome a short-term cash-flow shortage, and what each way costs.
items.canonical_answer: Three routes, each with a cost attached. An overdraft: spending beyond the balance up to an agreed limit, repayable as cash returns - its cost is interest on the amount used, plus whatever conditions a bank attaches, because the facility is the bank's to review. Delaying supplier payments: holding cash longer by paying at the end of the agreed window or beyond it - its cost sits in the relationship, with discounts lost and priority slipping when goods are scarce. Asking debtors to pay more quickly: deposits, cash-only terms or an early-settlement discount - its cost is revenue given away on every early payment and, if pressed too hard, customers who take their orders elsewhere. What the routes share is that each shifts the timing of cash rather than creating it, which is what makes them short-term remedies.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each route with its cost - overdraft interest, supplier discounts and goodwill, debtor discount or strain - and one mark for what the routes share: shifting timing rather than creating cash.

items.prompt: Explain how a fall in working capital can lead a business into trouble even while its sales and profit are unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: where the cushion of current assets over current liabilities falls - debtors paying more slowly, stock unsold, cash spent - the flows of money into the business slow even though its sales are unchanged. items.prompt: Explain the parts of working capital and why the measure matters to a business.
items.canonical_answer: The parts: current assets on one side - stock held for sale, debtors who owe the business money, and cash in hand and bank - and current liabilities on the other: the supplier invoices, overdraft and other bills due within a year. Working capital is what the first list exceeds the second by, which is what makes it the measure of day-to-day safety. It matters at both ends: too little, and wages or suppliers go unpaid even for a business with sound long-term prospects, because dated payments wait for no one; too much, and resources sit idle in slow stock or spare cash that could have earned a return elsewhere, so the business is safe but wasteful. What the measure includes for a manager is the cushion itself - read alongside the payment dates, the number that tells the business how much slack its daily running has.
marking_guidance: Features: award for the parts - stock, debtors and cash against bills due within a year - and one mark for what the measure includes at both ends: too little risks unpaid bills; too much sits idle.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "Working capital is just another word for cash." Explain the error in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The error is shrinking a broad measure to one part of it. In fact working capital is current assets less current liabilities - stock and debtors as well as cash, minus the bills due within a year - so a business can hold its whole working capital in slow stock and still have no cash to pay Friday's wages, which is where the confusion bites: the cash is the liquid part, wrongly treated here as the whole. The test that tells the two apart: ask what has to happen before the figure can pay a bill. Cash pays at once; stock must be sold and collected first, and the debts owed to the business must still be collected - working capital is the whole cushion, cash is the part of it ready to spend.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact working capital spans stock, debtors and cash less near-term bills, wrongly reduced to the cash alone.
Award the second mark for the test: what must happen before the figure can pay a bill?

items.prompt: Okaukuejo Coolers, a two-year-old drinks maker in northern Namibia, sells to shops on credit but pays its bottling supplier on delivery. Its forecast shows closing balances falling from N$9 000 to N$7 000 to N$5 000 across three months, and its working capital sits at N$8 000, of which N$6 500 is slow-moving stock. A hotel chain has offered a trial order, payable half on delivery and half sixty days later. Analyse Okaukuejo Coolers' position and recommend what the owner should do.
items.canonical_answer: Analysis: the forecast shows a slide rather than a dip - the closing balances fall by roughly N$2 000 each month, which points to outflows running ahead of inflows structurally rather than one heavy month. The working capital of N$8 000 looks positive, but N$6 500 of it is slow stock, so the liquid part - the cash and the debtors likely to pay soon - is thin, and a dated payment could still find the business short even with working capital in the black. The trial order's half on delivery improves the usual credit pattern, but the second half arrives sixty days later, so it feeds the far end of the slide, not its cause. Recommendation: change the flows first - press the shops for shorter credit terms or a small early-settlement discount, and slow the stock build - and take the hotel order, because its half-on-delivery payment helps the near months; hold the overdraft as the reserve rather than the plan. Judgement: the position is a slide with a thin liquid layer, so the remedies that matter are the ones that change the flows. Criterion: what decides it is whether the monthly fall can be turned within the credit terms the shops will accept. Counterargument: against pressing the shops, a discount costs revenue and customers can resist; against the order, the sixty-day second half deepens the very slide it is meant to relieve. Condition: the recommendation depends on the shops' response - if they refuse shorter terms, the business needs longer-term finance rather than a bigger overdraft.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award for a clear recommendation on the order and on changing the flows.
Context: award for using the facts - the N$2 000 monthly slide, the N$8 000 working capital with N$6 500 in slow stock, the half on delivery.
Criterion: award for naming what decides it - whether the monthly fall can be turned within acceptable credit terms.
Counterargument: award for the case against taking the order or against the borrowing-first route - the sixty-day second half feeds the slide.
